frames.narration: The owner starts release v3 of the checkout service. The policy says this service is risky, so another team's approver has already signed. The controller records who started it, who approved it and which signed build it is.

The controller starts the canary instances, plus a fresh group of old-version instances of the same size, and tells the eu router to send 1% of users to v3. Users are chosen by a hash of their id, so each one stays on the same version.

Both groups report error rate, latency and completed checkouts to the metrics store, tagged with the version. The controller waits 10 minutes of bake time. At 1% the canary has seen 400 requests, which is enough for a decision of this kind.

The analysis compares the two groups at the same time. The canary error rate is 1.5% and the baseline is 1.5%, a z score of 0.00 against a limit of 2.33. Latency at the 99th percentile is within 3%. The verdict is pass.

The controller advances the weight to 10% and, after another bake, to 50%. Each stage has its own verdict recorded in the audit log. When the eu region has passed 50% and soaked, it is promoted to 100%, and the next wave of regions is allowed to start.

Later, a different release, v4, is at 10% in its first region. Its canary shows a 2.8% error rate against 1.0% for the baseline, from 2,000 requests in each group. The z score is 4.17, far over the limit of 2.33, and the verdict is fail.

Without waiting for a person, the controller sets the weight of v4 to zero. All users are back on the old version within seconds, because that version was still running. The canary is scaled down, and the later waves never start.

The release is marked failed with the numbers, the error rates, the request counts and the time of the rollback, and the owner is told. Only the 2,000 canary requests of that one bake window saw v4 before it was removed.
